note.explanation: The scientific method is a sequence for investigating a problem: observe, suggest a hypothesis, test it, and use the results to develop explanations and predictions. Repeated successful testing may lead to a law, but scientific ideas can still be changed when new evidence appears.
examples: Observing a shadow leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
If the holes in a row of cardboards are aligned, torchlight passes through; if one cardboard is moved, the light is blocked.
note.checkAnswer: A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested and could potentially be shown to be false.
note.simple: Observe something, suggest an explanation, and test it. Use the evidence to improve the explanation and make predictions.

note.title: Scientific Method: From Observation to Law
steps: Identify or recognize an issue or a problem.
Gather information through observations of its various aspects.
Propose an explanation or a guess work known as hypothesis.
Perform experiment or collect evidences to test the hypothesis.
Record, organize and analyze gathered data, plotting and interpreting graphs to reach at a conclusion which is called a theory.
Repeated tests of the theory to wide range of similar issues then lead towards the formulation of a law.
note.answer: The scientific method uses observations and experiments to test hypotheses, build theories, make predictions, and, after repeated testing, formulate laws.

written.finalAnswer: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation or guess based on observations or experiments, made so that its logical results can be tested. For example, shadows of opaque objects form in the path of light because light travels in a straight line.

written.text: Distinguish between a theory and a law of Physics.
written.finalAnswer: A theory is a logical explanation of the causes and effects of an event in nature, developed after an assumption is successfully verified through careful experimentation. A law is a statement about the behaviour of nature that has been tested many times and generally accepted as true; it explains past observations and experiments and can predict other aspects of nature.

written.text: What is falsifiability concept? How is it important?
written.finalAnswer: Falsifiability means that a theory makes predictions that can be tested and potentially proven false. It is important because it prevents scientific theories from relying on vague, non-specific or untestable claims and distinguishes them from beliefs that cannot be experimentally tested.

written.text: What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world. Its steps are identifying a problem, gathering observations, proposing a hypothesis, testing it by experiment or evidence, recording and analysing data to reach a theory, and repeatedly testing the theory towards a law. For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line. Holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch; light is seen through them, but moving a cardboard blocks the light. This experiment supports the hypothesis and helps establish the theory that light travels in a straight line. Repeated testing in similar situations may lead to a law.

steps.why: A shadow is the observation that gives the investigation its starting point.
steps.text: Observation: A shadow of an opaque object is formed when it is placed in the path of light from the Sun or a lamp.

steps.text: Hypothesis: Shadows of opaque objects are formed in the path of light because light travels in a straight line.

steps.why: The aligned holes allow a direct test of whether light travels in a straight line.
steps.text: Place four cardboards, each with a hole, in a straight line, with the first hole in front of a torch.

steps.why: Seeing the torch through the holes shows that light passes along the aligned path.
steps.text: When we see through the holes in the cards, we can see the light of the torch.

example.question: How can the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line be tested using four cardboards and a torch?
example.answer: Align the holes in four cardboards in front of a torch; the light can be seen through them. Displace one cardboard and the light is blocked. This supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.

explain.title: Observation and hypothesis
explain.body: The first step is to observe a natural process and collect data. From those observations, suggest an explanation that can be tested: this is a hypothesis. For example, observing a shadow can lead to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.

explain.title: Experiment
explain.body: “Experiment is an organized repeatable process which is used to test the truth of a hypothesis.” In the cardboard example, aligned holes let torchlight pass, while a displaced hole blocks it.

explain.title: Theory and prediction
explain.body: After an assumption is successfully verified by careful experimentation, it becomes a theory that applies to similar phenomena. Careful analysis of a theory can then be used to predict unknown aspects of nature. If test results do not agree with a prediction, the hypothesis is changed or rejected.

explain.title: Falsifiability
explain.body: A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested and potentially proven false. This requirement prevents theories from relying on vague or untestable claims.

explain.title: Law
explain.body: “When a theory has been tested many times and generally accepted as true, it is called a law.” A law explains observations and experiments of the past and can predict other aspects of nature. Theories and laws may still be modified or disproved when science brings new facts and insights.

mistakes: Do not mix up an observation, which records what happens, with a hypothesis, which suggests an explanation.
Do not call a hypothesis a theory before it has been tested and successfully verified through careful experimentation.
Do not say that one successful test proves a prediction will always be correct; repeated tests over similar situations are important.
Do not describe a law as an unchangeable ultimate truth; the section says scientific theories and laws can be modified or disproved.
Do not confuse falsifiability with proving a theory false: it means the theory can be tested and could potentially be proven false.
